nameStory: This microscopic green alga gets its scientific name from the Greek words 'nephros' meaning kidney and 'kytos' meaning cell, referring to its distinctive kidney-shaped cells. It was named after Carl Adolph Agardh, a Swedish botanist who pioneered the study of algae in the early 1800s. While it lacks a true common name, algae enthusiasts sometimes call it simply 'kidney alga' for its telltale curved shape.
description: Nephrocytium agardhianum is a tiny single-celled green alga that you'll only see with a microscope or magnifying glass. Each cell is kidney-shaped or crescent-shaped and bright green in color, measuring just 10-20 micrometers across. These microscopic plants often cluster together in small colonies floating in freshwater ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. Despite their tiny size, they play an important role in aquatic ecosystems as food for small animals and oxygen producers.

idTips.label: Cell shape
idTips.description: Distinctive kidney or crescent shape when viewed under magnification, with a pronounced curved indentation on one side

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small at 10-20 micrometers - about 1/50th the width of a human hair

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright emerald green due to chlorophyll, often appearing as tiny green specks in water samples

idTips.label: Colony formation
idTips.description: Often found in small loose clusters of 2-8 cells floating freely in water

idTips.label: Chloroplast
idTips.description: Contains a single large green chloroplast that fills most of the cell, sometimes with a visible bright spot (pyrenoid)

habitat: Found in clean freshwater environments throughout New England including ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams. Prefers nutrient-rich waters with good light penetration where it can photosynthesize effectively. Often discovered in the shallow margins of water bodies where sunlight reaches the bottom, mixed with other microscopic algae and plankton.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin to grow as water temperatures warm and daylight hours increase, becoming more abundant in pond water samples.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm months when optimal light and temperature conditions support rapid reproduction through cell division.
seasonality.fall: Numbers typically decline as water temperatures drop and light levels decrease, though some populations may persist.
seasonality.winter: Largely dormant or absent from the water column, potentially surviving as resistant stages in sediment until spring warming.

funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, a single drop of pond water can contain thousands of these kidney-shaped cells, and they produce enough oxygen through photosynthesis that they're considered the 'invisible forests' of freshwater ecosystems!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other crescent-shaped algae like Selenastrum, but Nephrocytium has a more pronounced kidney shape with a deeper indentation and typically forms looser colonies. Remember: Nephrocytium has a 'notched kidney' shape while Selenastrum looks more like a simple crescent moon.
contextualKnowledge: This species is part of the green algae group that gave rise to land plants millions of years ago, making these tiny organisms distant relatives of trees and flowers. The extremely low observation count in New England (only 4 recorded) likely reflects the specialized equipment and expertise needed to identify microscopic algae rather than actual rarity.
compareHints: Compared to its relative Nephrocytium lunatum, N. agardhianum has a more pronounced kidney shape with a deeper indentation and tends to form smaller, looser colonies. The cells of N. agardhianum are also typically slightly smaller and more consistently curved than the sometimes more elongated cells of N. lunatum.
